prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian-language prose and poetry in which memory, the body and dream are built into a metaphysical project of exceptional imaginative range.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B050, a single credited name, Mircea Cărtărescu. Round 1 gave me no new literary evidence that overturns it, and I do not treat the fact that all six files name the same writer as evidence of merit. That would be circular. The case rests on the common criteria. The voice is distinctive and recognisable in long, densely patterned sentences. The formal achievement lies in large, internally structured architectures, not ornament. Imaginative and intellectual depth comes from making memory, the body and dream into one metaphysical project. A poetic origin and essay work suggest an oeuvre that is broader than the long novels. In answer to the chair's first question, the works I rely on are Blinding, the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy, and Solenoid, as publicly described. I rely on the poetry and essays only to establish generic breadth, not to carry the claim. I read Nobel's 'ideal tendency' as serious, uncompromising inquiry into inner and historical experience. That fits this body of work without any appeal to national or political symbolism. I have tightened the citation to name the Romanian language, as the chair's summary noted wording differences. I have not widened its scope. On the chair's last question, I see no reason of merit or citation to prefer no award (P000) this year. My reservations concern the evidence available to us, not the quality of the work. They would justify caution about which volumes the citation leans on. They do not justify withholding it. All of this rests on public knowledge. I have not read the texts in this session and have not independently verified any source.
statement.case_against: The reservation I weigh most is the one every colleague raised and nobody has settled. We do not know whether the late, very large volumes deepen the project or enlarge and repeat it. If a close reading of the whole corpus showed enclosure and recycling of motifs in the later books, the sustained-quality criterion would be weaker than I have assumed. The claim would then narrow to the major cycles, and a citation worded around the whole oeuvre would overreach. A second reservation is translation. The effect depends on long-breathed syntax and rhythm, which any rendering partly flattens. I cannot assess the Romanian directly from the supplied evidence and do not claim to. A third reservation is coverage. Our knowledge of the poetry, essays and early prose is thinner than of the novels, so the whole-oeuvre claim is partly inferred. I would ask that any committee text say which volumes it relies on, not imply a full reading.

responses.point: Olsson moved Cărtărescu to first place in round 1 and keeps Zurita (B009) as his first alternative. He concedes that he can demonstrate less from the translated corpus than he suspects about the poems' intensity. He also says a Zurita citation would have to be worded strictly around the written poems.
responses.response: I agree with his wording condition, and it answers the chair's question about B009. If Zurita is raised, the citation should rest on the written sequences, such as Purgatory and Anteparadise, and the landscape-scale interventions should be treated as an extension of the poems, not as separate literary credit. I still keep B009 as my first alternative because the voice and the sustained, decades-long project are not in doubt. I also accept his candid asymmetry between what can be shown and what is suspected. For me it is the right reason not to put a verse-dependent case first. Sequence, sound and positional effects are exactly what a committee reading in translation cannot test. I would change my view if a member who reads the Spanish showed that the written sequences carry the achievement on their own, apart from their historical occasion.

responses.point: Palm accepts Adonis's formal and linguistic significance within Arabic poetry, and that the essays belong to the same project. She ranked him seventh for evidentiary reasons. The prosodic renewal is what translation conveys least, so a judgment of the whole depends on a few translated volumes. She also asks how the essays should be weighed against the poetry in a citation.
responses.response: This objection lands, and it is why I want to be explicit about how far I rely on B013. I placed him third because of the scale of the linguistic achievement: remaking a poetic language through myth, fragmentation and dialogue with inherited forms. That is a literary criterion, not a political one. But I concede that I cannot judge the prosody that carries that claim, and I would not defend him as a leading choice without dependable Arabic-language readers. I keep him as my second alternative on literary significance, but I give that placement less weight than my first alternative. On essays versus poetry, I would keep the citation on the poetry and treat the essays as intellectual context. That avoids having to weigh two genres inside one short formula.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg keeps Cărtărescu first but insists that the committee test directly whether the very large late volumes are self-enclosed or repetitive, and that opening-rank agreement is not evidence of merit. He also says that if the committee has dependable Arabic-language readers, their judgment should outweigh his on Adonis, and he does not name Adonis among his alternatives.
responses.response: I agree on method. The late-volume question is the real test, and I would rather it be put to the specific books than assumed away in either direction. My own bias is to read recurrence in a large mythological architecture as a possible deepening, but I cannot rule out that it is plain repetition, and I will not claim otherwise. I also take the point on Adonis seriously. His not naming Adonis, and Palm's evidentiary doubts, make that placement my least secure alternative. I keep it only because I hold that the significance for a whole literary language is a real criterion. If the committee cannot call on readers of the Arabic, that argues for placing the case after more evidence is gathered, not for treating the question as closed.

responses.point: Mattson keeps Cărtărescu first and keeps NDiaye as an alternative. She values NDiaye's control and range across fiction and drama, and she accepts that the oeuvre is more compact. She read my round-1 point on the length of the volumes as an argument for reading the whole corpus, including the poetry and earlier prose, before treating the novels as the oeuvre.
responses.response: I agree that the length of the volumes argues for reading the poetry and earlier prose before calling the novels the oeuvre, and I want that to shape how we word the citation, not just how we talk about it. That is why I name prose and poetry together and do not claim more for the poetry than public knowledge supports. On NDiaye, my position is the same as in round 1. The controlled, uncanny register and the range into drama are distinctive. I still put her below the large-scale case on cumulative weight and breadth, and I cannot assess the drama myself. The chair has asked you which works carry her case across decades. Your answer is the evidence that could change my ranking of her. A defensible account of how the later novels deepen the early fiction, without repeating it, would move her above my second alternative.

responses.point: Sward keeps Cărtărescu first and names Zurita and Tawada as alternatives. She treats Tawada as a linguistic and formal case that works at shorter scale. She says the repetition worry is the most serious qualification on her own first choice, and that it argues for judging the cycles as a whole rather than the late volumes alone.
responses.response: I agree that the cycles should be judged as wholes, and I would add that this applies to both sides of any comparison. Tawada's estrangement between Japanese and German is a real formal invention. But the question Sward raises herself, whether shorter, episodic forms sustain depth across a whole authorship, is one I cannot answer, since I did not place her in my own ranking. I will not fill that gap by guessing. I would reconsider only if members who read both languages showed depth that accumulates across the corpus. For now that leaves her outside my alternatives, though not outside the discussion.

uncertainties: Translation: how much of the density, rhythm and long syntax of Cărtărescu's Romanian survives in the translated editions the committee uses, and whether any member can judge the originals.

Whether the late, very large volumes deepen the earlier project or repeat its motifs. I cannot settle this without a close reading of the whole corpus, and no round-1 file offers verified close-reading evidence on either side.
Corpus coverage: the poetry, essays and early prose are thinner in translation and in my knowledge than the major novels, so the whole-oeuvre claim is partly inferred.
Whether Zurita's written sequences carry the case alone in Spanish, and how a citation can be limited to the written poems.
Whether Adonis's prosodic renewal can be judged adequately without Arabic readers, and how essays should be weighed against poetry.

My comparisons with candidates I ranked lower or did not rank (NDiaye, Yan Lianke, Wright, Tawada) rest on public knowledge, not independent verification, and could change if colleagues supply specific evidence about those corpora.

Carlberg's actual committee voting status as a co-opted member is undocumented, so her simulated vote is a modeling assumption. The full Swedish Academy makes the actual decision and is not simulated here.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent from the supplied profile, and nothing has changed since round 1. My own work is non-fiction and biography (what I call 'litterär sakprosa'), which is context and not evidence of a preference for any candidate. The profile records no personal, institutional or translation connection to any shortlisted writer. My marriage and my election to the Academy alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg create no tie to a candidate. I serve as co-opted member in my capacity as Permanent Secretary, and whether I vote in committee is undocumented. I disclose that and do not adjudicate it.
